osces.title: Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis - Diagnosis and Treatment
objectives: Diagnose allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) using diagnostic criteria
Interpret imaging findings, serology, and pulmonary function tests
Initiate corticosteroid therapy and monitor response
Discuss antifungal therapy (itraconazole) as steroid-sparing agent
Monitor for complications: bronchiectasis, pulmonary fibrosis
Differentiate ABPA from asthma exacerbation and eosinophilic pneumonia
osces.scenario_stem: You are a respiratory medicine registrar in the outpatient clinic. Mrs Priya Sharma, a 42-year-old woman with long-standing asthma, presents with worsening asthma control despite high-dose inhaled corticosteroids and LABAs. She has recurrent episodes of productive cough with brown mucus plugs, fleeting pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-rays, and peripheral eosinophilia. Her asthma has been difficult to control for the past 6 months. Recent investigations show total IgE 2,800 IU/mL (markedly elevated), positive Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgE and IgG, and central bronchiectasis on HRCT chest. Assess for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), confirm diagnosis, and initiate appropriate treatment.

patient_demographics.living_situation: Lives with husband and two teenage children in suburban Melbourne
patient_demographics.support_network: Supportive family, active in school community

presenting_complaint.chief_complaint: Worsening asthma control for 6 months, recurrent cough with brown sputum plugs, repeated chest X-ray infiltrates
presenting_complaint.duration: 6 months of progressive symptoms despite treatment escalation
presenting_complaint.severity: Asthma now poorly controlled despite high-dose ICS/LABA, requiring oral prednisolone courses every 4-6 weeks
presenting_complaint.pattern: Episodic worsening with fleeting pulmonary infiltrates, partial response to oral steroids, then recurrence
associated_symptoms: Productive cough with thick, brown, mucoid sputum (occasionally expectorates firm mucus plugs)
Wheeze (worse at night and early morning)
Dyspnoea (reduced exercise tolerance, unable to walk briskly without breathlessness)
presenting_complaint.impact_on_life: Missing work frequently (3-4 days/month due to asthma exacerbations), unable to participate in school sports events, reduced family activities

history_of_presenting_complaint.onset: Asthma diagnosed age 12, generally well-controlled until 6 months ago
history_of_presenting_complaint.progression: Progressive deterioration despite escalation of inhaled corticosteroids (fluticasone 500 mcg BD → fluticasone/salmeterol 500/50 mcg BD → budesonide/formoterol 400/12 mcg BD with additional as-needed use). Requires oral prednisolone 25-40 mg for 5-7 days every 4-6 weeks for exacerbations.
history_of_presenting_complaint.precipitating_factors: No clear triggers. Episodes not related to allergen exposure, viral infections, or exercise. No seasonal pattern.
history_of_presenting_complaint.relieving_factors: Oral prednisolone courses provide temporary improvement (2-4 weeks), then symptoms recur. Inhaled bronchodilators (salbutamol) provide minimal relief.
history_of_presenting_complaint.previous_episodes: Four exacerbations in past 6 months, each requiring oral prednisolone. Two ED presentations (treated and discharged). Chest X-rays during exacerbations showed changing pulmonary infiltrates (different locations each time - right upper lobe, left lower lobe, right middle lobe).
history_of_presenting_complaint.investigations_to_date: Chest X-rays x 4 (6 months): fleeting infiltrates, resolving between episodes. Spirometry 3 months ago: FEV1 68% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.65 (obstructive), reversibility 18% post-bronchodilator. HRCT chest (requested 2 weeks ago): central bronchiectasis (proximal airways), mucus impaction, no peripheral bronchiectasis. Full blood count: eosinophils 1.8 x 10⁹/L (elevated). Total IgE 2,800 IU/mL (normal <100). Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgE strongly positive. Aspergillus precipitins (IgG) positive.
history_of_presenting_complaint.treatments_tried: Multiple inhaler regimens (as above), oral prednisolone courses (partial response), montelukast 10 mg daily (no benefit, ceased), salbutamol as-needed (limited benefit).

conditions: Asthma diagnosed age 12 (childhood asthma, persisted into adulthood)
Allergic rhinitis (seasonal, responds to nasal corticosteroids)
No diabetes mellitus (relevant for corticosteroid therapy)
No cystic fibrosis (normal sweat test age 13 when investigated for recurrent respiratory infections)
hospitalisations: Admitted age 28 for severe asthma exacerbation (ICU admission, intubated for 2 days, recovered)
Two ED presentations in past 6 months (acute asthma, treated with nebulizers and oral prednisolone, discharged)

current.name: Budesonide/formoterol (Symbicort Turbuhaler)
current.frequency: 2 puffs twice daily + additional as needed for symptoms (MART regimen)

current.name: Prednisolone
current.frequency: once daily for 5-7 days during exacerbations

conditions: Mother: Asthma (mild, well-controlled with low-dose ICS)
No family history of cystic fibrosis, immunodeficiency, or fungal infections
family_history.genetic_risk: Family atopy (asthma, eczema, allergic rhinitis common)

occupation.exposure: School environment, chalk/dust exposure (now uses whiteboards), no laboratory chemical exposure, classrooms well-ventilated

exercise.baseline: Previously walked 30 minutes daily, yoga twice weekly
exercise.current: Reduced activity due to dyspnoea and fatigue

social_history.living_environment: Suburban house (15 years old), no visible mould, no damp areas. No pets (family dog died 2 years ago, not replaced). Air conditioning serviced regularly. Dehumidifier in bedrooms.

physical_examination.general_inspection: Well-appearing woman, not in respiratory distress at rest. No cyanosis. Talks in full sentences.

cardiovascular.inspection: JVP not elevated. No peripheral oedema.
cardiovascular.palpation: Apex beat palpable, not displaced. Peripheral pulses normal.

respiratory.inspection: Chest wall symmetrical, normal expansion. No use of accessory muscles at rest. No scars.
respiratory.palpation: Chest expansion symmetrical and adequate. Tactile fremitus normal. No tenderness.
respiratory.auscultation: Bilateral expiratory wheeze (widespread, polyphonic). Prolonged expiratory phase. Some coarse crackles in right upper zone. No bronchial breathing.

abdominal.inspection: Soft, no distension. Caesarean section scars visible (low transverse).
abdominal.palpation: Soft, non-tender. No organomegaly. No masses.

physical_examination.neurological: Alert and oriented. No focal neurological deficit. No cushingoid features (despite intermittent prednisolone use).
physical_examination.skin: No rashes. No eczema currently. No jaundice or pallor.
physical_examination.other: Nasal examination: pale, boggy nasal mucosa (allergic rhinitis). No nasal polyps visualized.

imaging.result: CENTRAL bronchiectasis involving proximal airways (bilateral upper lobes and right middle lobe). Dilated bronchi with bronchial wall thickening. Mucoid impaction visible in several dilated bronchi (high-attenuation mucus plugs - 'finger-in-glove' sign in right upper lobe bronchus). Tree-in-bud opacities in right upper lobe. No peripheral bronchiectasis. No cavitation. No pulmonary fibrosis. No ground-glass opacities currently (between exacerbations). Mild bronchial wall thickening throughout.
imaging.interpretation: CENTRAL bronchiectasis with mucoid impaction - HIGHLY SPECIFIC for ABPA. 'Finger-in-glove' sign pathognomonic. No active infiltrates currently (patient between exacerbations). CT findings meet ABPA diagnostic criteria.

imaging.result: Right upper lobe consolidation/infiltrate. Tramline shadows (dilated bronchi) visible in upper zones bilaterally. Previous CXRs (3, 4, 6 months ago): Left lower lobe infiltrate (3 months), right middle lobe infiltrate (4 months), clear (6 months). Fleeting infiltrates noted - different locations, resolving between episodes.
imaging.interpretation: Fleeting pulmonary infiltrates (migratory, transient) - characteristic of ABPA. Tramline shadows indicate bronchiectasis.

imaging.result: Clear lung fields. Bronchial wall thickening visible in upper zones ('tramlines'). No acute infiltrates. No consolidation.
imaging.interpretation: Resolution of infiltrates between exacerbations (typical ABPA pattern). Underlying bronchiectasis visible as tramline shadows.

laboratory.result: Haemoglobin 138 g/L (115-165). WCC 9.2 x 10⁹/L (4.0-11.0). Eosinophils 1.8 x 10⁹/L (0.04-0.4) - MARKEDLY ELEVATED (absolute eosinophilia >1.0 x 10⁹/L). Neutrophils 5.4 x 10⁹/L. Lymphocytes 1.6 x 10⁹/L. Platelets 285 x 10⁹/L.
laboratory.interpretation: Peripheral eosinophilia (eosinophils >1,000/microL) - ESSENTIAL criterion for ABPA diagnosis.

laboratory.result: 2,800 IU/mL (normal <100 IU/mL for adults) - MARKEDLY ELEVATED
laboratory.interpretation: Total IgE >1,000 IU/mL - ESSENTIAL diagnostic criterion for ABPA. Very high levels (>1,000) highly suggestive of ABPA in asthmatic patient.

laboratory.result: Strongly positive - 28.5 kU/L (normal <0.35 kU/L, positive >0.35 kU/L)
laboratory.interpretation: Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgE elevated - ESSENTIAL criterion for ABPA. Indicates Type I hypersensitivity (immediate) to Aspergillus.
Aspergillus-specific IgG antibodies - indicates Type III hypersensitivity (immune complex-mediated). Supports ABPA diagnosis (not essential, but commonly positive).
Mildly elevated - suggests ongoing inflammation (between exacerbations).

laboratory.result: Creatinine 68 μmol/L (45-90). eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m². Urea 4.5 mmol/L (2.5-7.5).
laboratory.interpretation: Normal renal function (important baseline before itraconazole therapy).

laboratory.result: Bilirubin 12 μmol/L (3-20). ALT 28 U/L (5-40). AST 24 U/L (5-40). ALP 68 U/L (30-110). GGT 32 U/L (5-55). Albumin 42 g/L (35-50).
laboratory.interpretation: Normal liver function (important baseline before itraconazole - hepatotoxicity risk).
Normal glucose (important baseline before long-term prednisolone therapy).

pulmonary_function.result: Pre-bronchodilator: FEV1 2.10 L (68% predicted), FVC 3.23 L (85% predicted), FEV1/FVC ratio 0.65 (obstructive). Post-bronchodilator (400 mcg salbutamol): FEV1 2.48 L (80% predicted), FVC 3.28 L (86% predicted). Reversibility: 18% improvement in FEV1 (380 mL absolute increase).
pulmonary_function.interpretation: Obstructive lung disease with significant bronchodilator reversibility (>12% and >200 mL) - consistent with asthma. Reduced baseline FEV1 indicates partially controlled asthma.

pulmonary_function.test: Fractional Exhaled Nitric Oxide (FeNO) - 3 months ago
pulmonary_function.interpretation: Markedly elevated FeNO - indicates eosinophilic airway inflammation. Supports diagnosis of allergic/eosinophilic asthma and ABPA.

microbiology.result: No bacterial pathogens isolated. Fungal culture: Aspergillus fumigatus isolated (light growth). No Candida species. No mycobacteria.
microbiology.interpretation: Aspergillus fumigatus isolated from sputum - supports ABPA diagnosis but NOT essential (only 40-60% of ABPA patients have positive fungal cultures). Isolation indicates colonization/sensitization.

other.result: Positive reactions: House dust mite (6 mm wheal), grass pollen (4 mm wheal), cat dander (3 mm wheal), Aspergillus fumigatus (8 mm wheal - LARGE reaction). Negative control: 0 mm. Positive control (histamine): 5 mm.
other.interpretation: Type I hypersensitivity (immediate) to Aspergillus fumigatus - very large wheal (>3 mm positive, >6 mm strongly positive). Consistent with ABPA.

key_findings: ABPA diagnostic criteria met: 1) Asthma (predisposing condition), 2) Total IgE >1,000 IU/mL (2,800), 3) Aspergillus-specific IgE elevated, 4) Peripheral eosinophilia >500/microL (1,800/microL), 5) Positive Aspergillus skin test, 6) Central bronchiectasis on HRCT (highly specific), 7) Fleeting pulmonary infiltrates on CXR
ABPA Stage: Acute/Active ABPA (Stage 1 - Acute) - currently between exacerbations but elevated IgE, eosinophilia, CT changes indicate active disease requiring treatment
Radiological hallmark: Central bronchiectasis with mucoid impaction ('finger-in-glove' sign on CT) - pathognomonic for ABPA
Immunological hallmark: Markedly elevated total IgE (2,800 IU/mL) + Aspergillus-specific IgE + precipitins (IgG)
Poorly controlled asthma despite high-dose ICS/LABA + frequent oral steroid courses (steroid-dependent asthma)
No evidence of invasive aspergillosis, aspergilloma, or chronic necrotizing aspergillosis (different Aspergillus-related diseases)

supporting_features: ABPA diagnostic criteria FULLY MET (see key findings above)
Central bronchiectasis (upper lobe predominance) - radiological hallmark
Fleeting pulmonary infiltrates - characteristic migratory pattern
Underlying asthma (90% of ABPA occurs in asthmatics, 10% in CF)
Steroid-responsive but steroid-dependent (exacerbations recur off steroids)

differential_diagnosis.likelihood: UNLIKELY (some overlapping features but key differences)
supporting_features: Peripheral eosinophilia (present in both ABPA and CEP)
against_features: CEP typically has PERIPHERAL infiltrates on CT ('photographic negative of pulmonary oedema' - peripheral distribution), NOT central bronchiectasis
Total IgE usually normal or mildly elevated in CEP, NOT >1,000 IU/mL
No Aspergillus sensitization in CEP (negative Aspergillus serology)
CEP does NOT cause central bronchiectasis or mucoid impaction
CT pattern in this case (central bronchiectasis) diagnostic of ABPA, not CEP

supporting_features: Eosinophilia can occur in severe asthma
against_features: Total IgE >1,000 IU/mL NOT typical of asthma alone (ABPA required to explain this)
Central bronchiectasis NOT a feature of asthma (specific to ABPA)
Fleeting infiltrates NOT seen in asthma exacerbations
Aspergillus sensitization with IgE and IgG not explained by asthma alone
Patient meets ABPA diagnostic criteria - diagnosis is ABPA complicating asthma
Aspergilloma requires PRE-EXISTING cavity (TB, sarcoidosis, bullae) - this patient has no cavities on CT
Aspergilloma appears as solid mass/ball within cavity on imaging ('air crescent sign')
Aspergilloma does NOT cause eosinophilia or elevated IgE
No haemoptysis (common in aspergilloma)
CT shows bronchiectasis and mucoid impaction, NOT aspergilloma
IPA occurs in IMMUNOCOMPROMISED patients (neutropenia, transplant, high-dose corticosteroids) - this patient is immunocompetent
IPA causes necrotizing pneumonia with cavitation, nodules, 'halo sign' on CT
IPA does NOT cause eosinophilia or elevated IgE (non-allergic infection)
Patient clinically well (not septic), no severe immunosuppression
CT findings incompatible with IPA (central bronchiectasis, not necrotizing lesions)

supporting_features: Marked eosinophilia (>1,500/microL for >6 months can indicate HES)
against_features: HES requires eosinophilia with END-ORGAN DAMAGE (heart, lungs, GI, CNS, skin) without secondary cause. This patient's eosinophilia is SECONDARY to ABPA (Aspergillus sensitization), not primary HES.
No cardiac involvement (endomyocardial fibrosis, which occurs in HES)
No skin, GI, or neurological manifestations of HES
Aspergillus serology positive - explains eosinophilia (allergic response to Aspergillus)
Diagnosis is ABPA (secondary eosinophilia), not HES (primary eosinophilia)

clinical_reasoning_points: ALLERGIC BRONCHOPULMONARY ASPERGILLOSIS (ABPA) is a hypersensitivity lung disease caused by immunological response to Aspergillus fumigatus (ubiquitous environmental fungus). Occurs almost exclusively in patients with asthma (90%) or cystic fibrosis (10%). Prevalence: 1-2% of asthmatics, up to 10% of severe/steroid-dependent asthmatics.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Aspergillus fungal spores inhaled → germinate in bronchial mucus (especially in asthma/CF where mucus clearance impaired) → release antigens → Type I hypersensitivity (IgE-mediated immediate reaction - bronchospasm, eosinophilia) + Type III hypersensitivity (immune complex-mediated, IgG-precipitins - inflammation, pulmonary infiltrates) → eosinophilic inflammation → mucus plugging → bronchiectasis (central, proximal airways).

DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA for ABPA (International Society for Human and Animal Mycology - ISHAM 2013 Consensus): ESSENTIAL criteria (must have ALL): 1) Predisposing condition (asthma or CF), 2) Total IgE >1,000 IU/mL (or >417 IU/mL if on corticosteroids), 3) Positive Aspergillus-specific IgE (skin test or serology). OTHER criteria (supportive, not all required): Peripheral eosinophilia >500/microL, Aspergillus precipitins (IgG), Radiological infiltrates (fleeting), Central bronchiectasis on HRCT.

RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES: Central bronchiectasis (involves proximal/segmental bronchi, spares peripheral airways) - HIGHLY SPECIFIC for ABPA, distinguishes from other causes of bronchiectasis (which typically affect peripheral airways). Mucoid impaction ('finger-in-glove' sign, 'toothpaste sign', 'gloved-finger opacity') - pathognomonic. Fleeting pulmonary infiltrates (migratory, transient, resolve spontaneously or with steroids). High-attenuation mucus on CT (mucus appears BRIGHT on CT due to high protein, eosinophil, and fungal content).

ABPA STAGES (Staging system helps guide treatment): Stage 1 (Acute) - active disease, elevated IgE, eosinophilia, infiltrates. Stage 2 (Remission) - asymptomatic, IgE decreased >35% from baseline, no infiltrates. Stage 3 (Exacerbation) - recurrence after remission, IgE increased >50% from remission baseline. Stage 4 (Corticosteroid-dependent asthma) - requires continuous steroids to control asthma. Stage 5 (Fibrotic) - irreversible pulmonary fibrosis, end-stage disease. This patient: Stage 1 (Acute) requiring treatment initiation.

TREATMENT - PRIMARY: CORTICOSTEROIDS (prednisolone) are FIRST-LINE treatment. Regimen: Prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day (30-40 mg daily for most adults) for 2-4 weeks, then taper over 3-6 months (e.g., reduce by 5-10 mg every 2 weeks) while monitoring IgE levels. Goals: Suppress immune response, reduce eosinophilia, clear infiltrates, prevent bronchiectasis progression.

TREATMENT - ADJUNCTIVE: ITRACONAZOLE (antifungal) as steroid-sparing agent. Reduces fungal burden (fewer antigens → less immune stimulation). Dose: 200 mg BD for 16 weeks (some protocols use 6-12 months). Benefit: Allows lower steroid doses, reduces exacerbations. PBS criteria in Australia: ABPA confirmed by specialist, failed steroid taper, or steroid-dependent. Monitoring: LFTs (hepatotoxicity), serum itraconazole levels (ensure therapeutic range 0.5-4 mg/L). Note: Itraconazole interacts with many drugs (CYP3A4 inhibitor) - check drug interactions.

MONITORING RESPONSE: Total IgE is the PRIMARY biomarker for monitoring treatment response. Measure every 1-2 months during treatment. Treatment success: IgE decreases >35% from baseline after 2-3 months, eosinophil count normalizes, CXR infiltrates clear, FEV1 improves. If IgE increases >50% or new infiltrates develop → exacerbation, increase steroids.

ASTHMA OPTIMIZATION: Continue high-dose ICS/LABA to control underlying asthma. ABPA treatment (steroids + itraconazole) often dramatically improves asthma control. Consider biologics (omalizumab, mepolizumab, benralizumab) if asthma remains severe despite ABPA treatment - biologics show benefit in ABPA (reduce exacerbations, steroid requirements).

COMPLICATIONS if untreated: Progressive central bronchiectasis → irreversible lung damage. Pulmonary fibrosis (Stage 5 ABPA) → chronic respiratory failure. Aspergilloma formation in bronchiectatic cavities → haemoptysis. Steroid-dependent asthma → Cushingoid side effects, osteoporosis, diabetes.

PROGNOSIS: With treatment, most patients achieve remission (Stage 2) within 6-12 months. However, 50% experience exacerbations over 5-10 years (Stage 3) requiring repeat steroid courses. Continuous monitoring (annual IgE, spirometry, CXR) essential. Early treatment prevents progression to fibrotic stage.

DIFFERENTIAL - ABPA vs ASPERGILLUS-RELATED DISEASES: 1) ABPA - allergic/immune-mediated, asthma/CF, elevated IgE, eosinophilia, central bronchiectasis. 2) Aspergilloma - saprophytic colonization of pre-existing cavity, normal IgE, no eosinophilia, 'fungal ball' on imaging. 3) Invasive Aspergillosis - invasive infection, immunocompromised, necrotizing pneumonia, no eosinophilia. 4) Chronic Necrotizing Aspergillosis - semi-invasive, mildly immunocompromised, cavitation, chronic course.

red_flags.flag: Undiagnosed ABPA for 6+ months (progressive central bronchiectasis developing - irreversible lung damage)
red_flags.action: URGENT initiation of corticosteroid therapy to halt bronchiectasis progression. Delay in treatment leads to permanent lung damage (fibrotic ABPA, Stage 5, untreatable).

red_flags.flag: Steroid-dependent asthma (requiring oral prednisolone every 4-6 weeks) without ABPA diagnosis/treatment
red_flags.action: Patient has been receiving intermittent steroids (treating symptomatically) without addressing underlying ABPA. Needs SUSTAINED steroid course (3-6 months taper) + itraconazole to achieve remission and prevent exacerbations.

red_flags.flag: Total IgE 2,800 IU/mL (markedly elevated) - indicates severe allergic/immune response
red_flags.action: Very high IgE levels suggest active, severe ABPA. Requires aggressive treatment. Monitor IgE every 1-2 months during treatment (should decrease >35% with successful therapy).

red_flags.flag: Peripheral eosinophilia 1.8 x 10⁹/L (could indicate hypereosinophilic syndrome if not treated)
red_flags.action: Although secondary eosinophilia due to ABPA, prolonged severe eosinophilia can cause END-ORGAN DAMAGE (heart, lungs). Corticosteroid treatment will reduce eosinophils. Monitor FBC, echocardiogram if eosinophilia persists >6 months despite treatment.

red_flags.flag: Recurrent pulmonary infiltrates (could be misdiagnosed as recurrent pneumonia, leading to unnecessary antibiotics)
red_flags.action: Fleeting infiltrates in ABPA are NON-INFECTIOUS (eosinophilic inflammation, not bacterial). DO NOT treat with antibiotics. Educate patient: future infiltrates likely ABPA exacerbations requiring steroid increase, not antibiotics.

learning_outcomes: Recognize clinical presentation of ABPA: poorly controlled asthma, recurrent infiltrates, brown mucus plugs, eosinophilia
Apply ABPA diagnostic criteria (ISHAM 2013): total IgE >1,000 IU/mL, Aspergillus-specific IgE, eosinophilia, central bronchiectasis
Interpret HRCT findings: central bronchiectasis, mucoid impaction ('finger-in-glove' sign), high-attenuation mucus
Differentiate ABPA from other Aspergillus-related diseases (aspergilloma, invasive aspergillosis, chronic necrotizing aspergillosis)
Initiate corticosteroid therapy: prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day, taper over 3-6 months, monitor IgE response
Prescribe itraconazole as steroid-sparing agent: 200 mg BD for 16 weeks, monitor LFTs and drug levels
Understand ABPA staging system and treatment goals for each stage
Monitor treatment response using total IgE (biomarker), eosinophil count, spirometry, imaging
Recognize complications: progressive bronchiectasis, pulmonary fibrosis (Stage 5 ABPA), aspergilloma formation
Discuss prognosis: achievable remission with treatment, but 50% experience exacerbations requiring long-term monitoring

key_tasks: Recognize ABPA based on clinical presentation and confirm diagnosis using ISHAM criteria
Interpret investigations: total IgE >1,000 IU/mL, Aspergillus-specific IgE positive, eosinophilia >500/microL, HRCT central bronchiectasis
Initiate prednisolone therapy: dose 0.5 mg/kg/day (30-40 mg daily), duration 2-4 weeks then taper over 3-6 months
Discuss itraconazole as steroid-sparing agent: indications, dose, duration, monitoring (LFTs, drug levels)
Explain ABPA pathophysiology to patient (allergic reaction to Aspergillus fungus causing lung inflammation)
Outline monitoring plan: total IgE every 1-2 months (goal >35% reduction), eosinophil count, spirometry, CXR/CT
Discuss prognosis: good with treatment (remission achievable), but requires long-term monitoring (exacerbations common)
Address asthma optimization: continue high-dose ICS/LABA, expect improvement in asthma control with ABPA treatment
Educate about fleeting infiltrates: not infections, do not require antibiotics, indicate ABPA exacerbations
Arrange follow-up: 4-6 weeks (assess response, adjust steroid taper, check IgE)
candidate_challenges: Recognizing ABPA (uncommon diagnosis, requires high index of suspicion in poorly controlled asthma)
Differentiating ABPA from chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, hypereosinophilic syndrome, and severe asthma alone
Understanding ABPA diagnostic criteria (ISHAM 2013) and knowing total IgE threshold (>1,000 IU/mL)
Interpreting HRCT findings: central vs peripheral bronchiectasis (central specific for ABPA)
Prescribing appropriate steroid regimen (dose, duration, taper schedule)
Knowing when to add itraconazole (steroid-sparing, not first-line monotherapy)
Understanding IgE monitoring as primary biomarker for treatment response
Communicating complex pathophysiology and long-term management plan clearly to patient
pass_criteria: Diagnoses ABPA using ISHAM criteria: asthma + IgE >1,000 + Aspergillus-specific IgE + eosinophilia + central bronchiectasis
Initiates prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day (30-40 mg for this patient), explains 2-4 week course then taper over 3-6 months
Discusses itraconazole 200 mg BD as steroid-sparing agent, mentions PBS criteria, monitoring LFTs and drug levels
Explains IgE monitoring (every 1-2 months, goal >35% reduction from baseline)
Differentiates ABPA from aspergilloma (cavity + fungal ball), invasive aspergillosis (immunocompromised), CEP (peripheral infiltrates)
Discusses prognosis: remission achievable within 6-12 months, but 50% experience exacerbations requiring monitoring
Optimizes asthma management: continue ICS/LABA, expect improvement in control with ABPA treatment
Arranges appropriate follow-up: 4-6 weeks (assess response, check IgE, adjust steroids)
common_errors: Failing to recognize ABPA (diagnosing as 'refractory asthma' without investigating underlying cause)
Confusing ABPA with aspergilloma or invasive aspergillosis (different Aspergillus diseases)
Not checking total IgE (misses essential diagnostic criterion)
Prescribing antibiotics for fleeting infiltrates (incorrect - infiltrates are eosinophilic, not infectious)
Under-dosing prednisolone or using too short a course (inadequate treatment, risk of relapse)
Not adding itraconazole in steroid-dependent patient (misses opportunity to reduce steroid burden)
Not monitoring IgE levels to assess treatment response (IgE is primary biomarker)
Confusing central bronchiectasis (ABPA) with peripheral bronchiectasis (other causes)

marking_criteria.criterion: Recognizes and diagnoses ABPA using ISHAM criteria
marking_criteria.description: States diagnosis of ABPA. Lists diagnostic criteria met: 1) Asthma (predisposing condition), 2) Total IgE >1,000 IU/mL (2,800 meets threshold), 3) Aspergillus-specific IgE positive, 4) Peripheral eosinophilia >500/microL (1,800), 5) Central bronchiectasis on HRCT (highly specific). Explains these findings confirm ABPA.

Identifies central bronchiectasis (proximal airways, upper lobe predominance) as hallmark of ABPA. Recognizes mucoid impaction ('finger-in-glove' sign) as pathognomonic. Differentiates from peripheral bronchiectasis (other causes). States central bronchiectasis is HIGHLY SPECIFIC for ABPA.

Prescribes prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day (approximately 30-40 mg daily for this patient, weight 72 kg). Explains regimen: 2-4 weeks at full dose, then taper gradually over 3-6 months (e.g., reduce by 5-10 mg every 2 weeks). Mentions monitoring during taper: IgE levels, eosinophil count, symptoms, spirometry. Goal: achieve remission (IgE decrease >35%).

Recommends itraconazole 200 mg BD for 16 weeks (or longer, 6-12 months in some protocols). Explains rationale: reduces fungal burden, less antigen exposure, allows lower steroid doses, reduces exacerbations. Mentions PBS criteria: specialist-confirmed ABPA, failed steroid taper or steroid-dependent. Discusses monitoring: baseline and regular LFTs (hepatotoxicity risk), serum itraconazole levels (therapeutic range 0.5-4 mg/L), check drug interactions (CYP3A4 inhibitor).

marking_criteria.criterion: Outlines monitoring plan for treatment response
marking_criteria.description: Primary biomarker: Total IgE measured every 1-2 months during treatment. Success criteria: IgE decreases >35% from baseline (target <1,000 IU/mL), eosinophil count normalizes, infiltrates clear on CXR, FEV1 improves. Exacerbation criteria: IgE increases >50% or new infiltrates → increase steroids. Follow-up spirometry, CXR at 3-6 months.

marking_criteria.criterion: Differentiates ABPA from other Aspergillus-related diseases
marking_criteria.description: Distinguishes: 1) ABPA - allergic, asthma/CF, elevated IgE, central bronchiectasis. 2) Aspergilloma - fungal ball in pre-existing cavity, normal IgE, no eosinophilia. 3) Invasive aspergillosis - immunocompromised, necrotizing lesions, no eosinophilia. 4) Chronic necrotizing aspergillosis - semi-invasive, cavitation, chronic. States this patient has ABPA based on diagnostic criteria.

Continues high-dose ICS/LABA (budesonide/formoterol). Explains ABPA treatment will improve asthma control (many patients have dramatic improvement once ABPA treated). Educates: fleeting infiltrates are ABPA exacerbations, not infections - do NOT require antibiotics. Consider biologic therapy (omalizumab, mepolizumab) if asthma remains severe despite ABPA treatment.

Prognosis: With treatment, most achieve remission (Stage 2) within 6-12 months. However, 50% experience exacerbations (Stage 3) over 5-10 years requiring repeat steroid courses. Long-term monitoring essential: annual IgE, spirometry, CXR. Early treatment prevents progression to fibrotic stage (Stage 5 - irreversible lung damage). Emphasizes importance of adherence and follow-up.

marking_criteria.criterion: Educates patient about ABPA and treatment
marking_criteria.description: Explains ABPA in simple terms: 'Allergic reaction to Aspergillus fungus (mould) in lungs causing inflammation, mucus plugs, and lung damage. Not an infection - your immune system overreacts to the fungus.' Explains treatment: steroids suppress immune reaction, antifungal reduces fungus, allowing lower steroid doses. Realistic expectations: improvement likely, but long-term monitoring needed. Addresses patient questions and concerns.

marking_criteria.criterion: Addresses medication side effects and monitoring
marking_criteria.description: Discusses prednisolone side effects: weight gain, glucose intolerance, mood changes, osteoporosis (long-term). Monitoring: fasting glucose (baseline and during treatment, risk of steroid-induced diabetes), bone density (DEXA scan if prolonged steroids >3 months), gastric protection (PPI if GERD or gastritis risk). Itraconazole: hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs), drug interactions (check all medications).

marking_criteria.criterion: Arranges appropriate follow-up and specialist input
marking_criteria.description: Follow-up: 4-6 weeks to assess response (IgE, eosinophils, symptoms, spirometry).
